What is the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis code for this patient?

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:
Admitting Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
A 60-year-old female presented to the emergency room with a sudden onset of severe headache associated with vomiting. On the administration of a CT scan of the brain, subarachnoid hemorrhage was observed, and an aneurysm was suspected. The patient underwent CT cerebral angiogram, and a bilobed anterior communicating artery aneurysm was discovered, projecting anterosuperiorly with a size of 8 x 7 x 5 mm. On the fourth day of ictus, the patient underwent right pterional craniotomy and clipping of the aneurysm. Following surgery, the patient developed right-sided ptosis that advanced to complete right-sided oculomotor nerve paralysis with a dilated and nonreacting pupil. A CT scan of the brain was performed, but no hematoma or infarct was noted. The patient was discharged on the eighth postoperative day and kept under regular follow-up in our outpatient department.

Discharge Condition:
Stable with recovered oculomotor nerve paralysis.

Course of Treatment:
The patient was administered antiedema measures, anticonvulsant, analgesic, and Nimodipine. The medication was continued for a total of 21 days following the ictus.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with their healthcare provider regularly.

Follow-up Care:
The patient underwent a Magnetic Resonance Imaging scan of the brain with venogram to rule out any infarct or thrombosis of the cavernous sinus after a week of discharge. No abnormalities were noted. The patient came for follow-up on the 61st postoperative day, and her ptosis had fully recovered. A full recovery of the ocular motor nerve paralysis was noted. The patient was advised to continue regular follow-up with their healthcare provider.

Discharge Medications:
Medications are not listed as per case report instructions.

text:
**Principal diagnosis code: I60.7 – Subarachnoid haemorrhage from intracranial artery, unspecified**

This is the code I would assign, but ICD-10-AM has a more specific option that I think fits better.

**Reasoning**
- The patient was admitted with a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm. The sudden severe headache and vomiting, the CT showing SAH, and the angiogram finding the aneurysm all support this.
- The condition chiefly responsible for the admission and treated by clipping is the ruptured aneurysm.
- ICD-10-AM classifies SAH from a specific artery to I60.-. The anterior communicating artery has its own code, **I60.2 – Subarachnoid haemorrhage from anterior communicating artery**. This is more specific than I60.7, so **I60.2** is the correct principal diagnosis.

**Final answer: I60.2** (Subarachnoid haemorrhage from anterior communicating artery)

**Additional diagnoses**
- Postoperative oculomotor (third) nerve palsy: H49.0 (Third [oculomotor] nerve palsy), together with a complication code such as G97.8 (Other intraoperative and postprocedural disorders of nervous system). Coders should check the current edition for the exact choice, and add a Y83.- or Y60-Y69 external cause code if required.
- Ptosis is integral to the nerve palsy and is not coded separately.

**Procedure (ACHI)**
- Craniotomy with clipping of the intracranial aneurysm (block 1 of ACHI, intracranial vascular procedures).
- CT cerebral angiogram and MRI/MR venogram as applicable.

The ICD-10-AM code set is updated by edition, so verify the codes against your local edition and coding standards.
